We characterize a natural class of modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension as representation categories of twisted doubles of finite p-groups. We also show that a nilpotent braided fusion category C admits an analogue of the Sylow decomposition. If the simple objects of C have integral Frobenius-Perron dimensions then C is group-theoretical. As a consequence, we obtain that semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension are group-theoretical. Our arguments are based on a reconstruction of twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories (this is reminiscent to the characterization of doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras in terms of Manin pairs).

We also show that a nilpotent braided fusion category \(\mathcal{C}\) admits an analogue of the Sylow decomposition. If the simple objects of \(\mathcal{C}\) have integral Frobenius–Perron dimensions, then \(\mathcal{C}\) is group-theoretical. As a consequence, we prove that semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime-power dimension are group-theoretical. Our arguments are based on a reconstruction of twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories, reminiscent of the characterization of doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras in terms of Manin pairs.
outputs.L2: We identify a natural family of modular categories whose Frobenius-Perron dimensions are powers of a prime, showing that they arise as representation categories of twisted quantum doubles of finite \(p\)-groups. We further prove that a nilpotent braided fusion category \(\mathcal{C}\) has a counterpart of the Sylow decomposition. When every simple object in \(\mathcal{C}\) has integral Frobenius-Perron dimension, the category is group-theoretical. It follows in particular that semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras with prime-power dimension are group-theoretical. The proofs rely on reconstructing twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories inside modular categories, in a way analogous to describing doubles of quasi-Lie bialgebras via Manin pairs.

The text studies structural properties of nilpotent braided fusion categories and modular categories whose Frobenius-Perron dimensions have prime-power form. A central result is the characterization of certain modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension as representation categories of twisted Drinfeld doubles of finite \(p\)-groups. In other words, under the appropriate hypotheses, these modular categories can be realized as
\[
\operatorname{Rep}(D^\omega G),
\]
where \(G\) is a finite \(p\)-group and \(D^\omega G\) denotes the twisted quantum double associated to a 3-cocycle \(\omega\) on \(G\).

A key ingredient in the analysis is an analogue of the classical Sylow decomposition for nilpotent braided fusion categories. Just as finite nilpotent groups decompose into products of their Sylow \(p\)-subgroups, nilpotent braided fusion categories can be decomposed into tensor products of subcategories whose Frobenius-Perron dimensions are powers of distinct primes. This provides a powerful reduction technique: many questions about general nilpotent braided fusion categories can be studied prime by prime.

The text further proves that nilpotent braided fusion categories whose simple objects all have integral Frobenius-Perron dimension are group-theoretical. This means that such categories are Morita equivalent to pointed fusion categories, or equivalently, they arise from finite group data in a precise categorical sense. The integrality assumption is essential in ensuring that the category has enough algebraic structure to be controlled by group-theoretical methods.

As a consequence, the results imply that every semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra of prime power dimension is group-theoretical. Since the representation category of a semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra is a fusion category, the categorical results apply directly to these algebras. Thus, quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension are shown to be governed by finite group-theoretical constructions, generalizing known results from Hopf algebra theory.

The arguments rely heavily on the reconstruction of twisted group doubles from Lagrangian subcategories of modular categories. A Lagrangian subcategory is a maximal symmetric fusion subcategory whose Frobenius-Perron dimension is the square root of that of the ambient modular category. The presence of such a subcategory allows one to identify the modular category with the representation category of a twisted double of a finite group. In the prime-power setting, this group is necessarily a \(p\)-group, leading to the stated characterization.

The study focuses on braided fusion categories whose Frobenius-Perron dimension is a power of a prime, with particular attention to the modular and nilpotent cases. A central theme is the use of Lagrangian subcategories as a reconstruction tool. When a modular category contains a suitable Lagrangian subcategory, it can often be realized as the representation category of the twisted Drinfeld double of a finite group. In the prime-power setting considered here, this group is shown to be a finite \(p\)-group, and the modular category is therefore identified with  
\[
\operatorname{Rep}(D^{\omega}G),
\]
the representation category of the twisted quantum double of a finite \(p\)-group \(G\), for an appropriate 3-cocycle \(\omega\).

This approach provides a structural description of modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension and connects them directly to finite group theory. In particular, it shows that such categories are not arbitrary: under the nilpotence and integrality assumptions, they arise from group-theoretical data. The presence of Lagrangian subcategories plays the role of detecting when a modular category is equivalent, in the braided sense, to the center of a pointed fusion category. Since the center of a pointed fusion category is precisely the representation category of a twisted double, the problem is reduced to understanding finite \(p\)-groups and their cohomological twists.

The results also imply that integral nilpotent braided fusion categories are group-theoretical. This is a strong structural conclusion, because group-theoretical fusion categories form a well-understood class built from finite groups, cocycles, and module categories. Thus, nilpotence together with integrality forces the category to behave much like a category coming from finite group data, even if it is not initially presented in that form.

A further consequence concerns semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension. The representation categories of such algebras are shown to be group-theoretical as well. This extends known classification and decomposition results for fusion categories and places these quasi-Hopf algebras within the group-theoretical framework. In this sense, the results generalize Sylow-type phenomena from finite group theory to the setting of fusion categories: prime-power dimensional components have a controlled and classifiable structure analogous to \(p\)-groups.

Overall, the work significantly advances the classification of fusion categories of prime power dimension. It demonstrates that modular and nilpotent braided fusion categories in this setting can be reconstructed from Lagrangian subcategories and identified with categories associated to twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups. Consequently, integral nilpotent braided fusion categories, as well as semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension, are shown to be group-theoretical. This strengthens the bridge between fusion category theory, finite group theory, and the theory of quasi-Hopf algebras.

The names Frobenius, Perron, and Sylow are associated with some of the most important ideas in algebra and linear theory. Although they arise in different contexts, they all reflect a central theme in mathematics: understanding complicated structures by identifying special substructures or dominant patterns.

The **Frobenius** name appears in several areas of mathematics. In group theory, the **Frobenius theorem** concerns special finite groups called Frobenius groups, which have a nontrivial subgroup acting in a highly regular way on the remaining elements. In linear algebra and matrix theory, Frobenius is also connected to the **Perron–Frobenius theorem**, one of the fundamental results about matrices with nonnegative entries.

The **Perron–Frobenius theorem** states that a square matrix with positive, or more generally nonnegative, entries has a distinguished real eigenvalue that dominates the others in size under suitable conditions. This eigenvalue is called the **Perron root**, and it has an eigenvector whose entries can be chosen to be positive. This result has many applications, including probability theory, dynamical systems, economics, graph theory, and the study of Markov chains. For example, it explains why certain long-term behaviors in networks or stochastic processes stabilize around a dominant pattern.

The name **Sylow** belongs primarily to finite group theory. The **Sylow theorems** describe the existence and behavior of subgroups whose orders are powers of primes. If a prime power divides the order of a finite group in a maximal way, then Sylow’s theorems guarantee the existence of subgroups of that order, called **Sylow subgroups**. They also explain how many such subgroups can exist and how they are related by conjugation. These theorems are essential tools for classifying finite groups and understanding their internal structure.

Together, Frobenius, Perron, and Sylow represent powerful methods for extracting order from complex mathematical objects. Frobenius and Perron reveal dominant eigenvalues and invariant directions in matrices and transformations, while Sylow’s theorems identify prime-power building blocks inside finite groups. Each theory shows that even within highly complicated systems, there are special elements, subgroups, or eigenvectors that control much of the overall structure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on modular categories of prime power Frobenius-Perron dimension, nilpotent braided fusion categories, Sylow-type decompositions, and group-theoretical quasi-Hopf algebras.
counterfactuals.output:
We study braided fusion categories of prime power Frobenius–Perron dimension, with particular emphasis on modular and nilpotent cases. Using the interaction between the Müger center, universal grading, and the adjoint subcategory, we establish Sylow-type decomposition results for nilpotent braided fusion categories and describe how such decompositions constrain the structure of modular categories of dimension \(p^{n}\). In particular, we show that prime power modular categories admit strong structural restrictions analogous to those for finite \(p\)-groups, and we identify conditions under which they decompose into tensor products of smaller braided factors.

We further relate these categorical decompositions to the representation theory of finite-dimensional semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras. We show that, in the nilpotent setting, the associated fusion categories are group-theoretical under natural hypotheses, and we describe the corresponding quasi-Hopf algebras in terms of finite groups, cohomological data, and equivariantization/de-equivariantization procedures. These results provide a categorical analogue of Sylow theory and clarify the role of prime power dimension in the classification of modular categories and group-theoretical quasi-Hopf algebras.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a mathematical paper proving that modular categories of prime power FP dimension arise as representation categories of twisted doubles of finite p-groups.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s central conclusion is that **integral modular categories whose Frobenius–Perron dimension is a prime power are not exotic: they come from finite \(p\)-groups**. More precisely, under the usual integrality hypotheses, a modular category \(\mathcal C\) with

\[
\operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C)=p^n
\]

is shown to be **group-theoretical**, and in fact braided equivalent to the representation category of a **twisted Drinfeld double** of a finite \(p\)-group:

\[
\mathcal C \simeq \operatorname{Rep}(D^\omega G)
\]

for some finite \(p\)-group \(G\) and some \(3\)-cocycle \(\omega \in Z^3(G,\mathbb C^\times)\).

Equivalently,

\[
\mathcal C \simeq Z(\operatorname{Vec}_G^\omega),
\]

the Drinfeld center of the pointed fusion category of \(G\)-graded vector spaces with associator twisted by \(\omega\).

The main results can be summarized as follows.

1. **Prime-power modular categories are nilpotent.**  
   The paper proves that modular categories of prime-power FP dimension have a strong nilpotence property. This heavily restricts their possible fusion rules and categorical structure.

2. **Integral such categories contain large symmetric subcategories.**  
   A key step is showing that an integral modular category of \(p\)-power dimension contains nontrivial Tannakian subcategories, typically equivalent to \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\) for some finite \(p\)-group \(H\).

3. **Existence of a Lagrangian subcategory.**  
   The authors show that the category contains a maximal symmetric, or Lagrangian, subcategory \(\mathcal L\), satisfying

   \[
   \mathcal L = \mathcal L',
   \]

   where \(\mathcal L'\) is the Müger centralizer. The existence of such a Lagrangian subcategory is the decisive criterion implying that the modular category is a Drinfeld center.

4. **Identification as a twisted double.**  
   By known reconstruction theorems, a modular category with a Lagrangian subcategory is equivalent to the center of a pointed fusion category. Thus

   \[
   \mathcal C \simeq Z(\operatorname{Vec}_G^\omega)
   \]

   for a finite group \(G\). Since the total FP dimension is a power of \(p\), \(G\) must be a finite \(p\)-group.

5. **Reduction of classification to finite \(p\)-groups and \(3\)-cocycles.**  
   The classification problem for these modular categories is therefore reduced to group cohomological data: finite \(p\)-groups \(G\) together with twisting classes

   \[
   [\omega] \in H^3(G,\mathbb C^\times).
   \]

6. **No genuinely new modular categories in this integral prime-power setting.**  
   The result rules out the existence of “exotic” integral modular categories of prime-power dimension. Every such category is group-theoretical and comes from a twisted quantum double construction.

A caveat is that the integrality assumption is essential. Nonintegral modular categories of prime-power FP dimension, such as semion or Ising-type categories in small dimensions, are not representation categories of twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups in this sense.

Given a modular category \(\mathcal C\), a Lagrangian subcategory \(\mathcal L \subset \mathcal C\) is a maximal symmetric fusion subcategory satisfying \(\mathcal L=\mathcal L'\), where \(\mathcal L'\) denotes its Müger centralizer. Such subcategories identify \(\mathcal C\) with the Drinfeld center of a pointed fusion category. Consequently, \(\mathcal C\) can be reconstructed as the representation category of a twisted quantum double \(D^{\omega}(G)\), for a finite group \(G\) and a cohomology class \(\omega \in H^{3}(G,k^{\times})\). The group \(G\) and associator twist \(\omega\) arise from the Tannakian data encoded by \(\mathcal L\) and the corresponding module-category or de-equivariantization construction.

This perspective gives a structural method for classifying semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras whose representation categories are modular. In particular, for quasi-Hopf algebras of prime power dimension, the existence of suitable Lagrangian subcategories often forces the representation category to be group-theoretical, hence Morita equivalent to a pointed fusion category. Their Drinfeld centers are therefore equivalent to categories of \(D^{\omega}(G)\)-modules for finite \(p\)-groups \(G\). This links categorical properties such as isotropic and Lagrangian subcategories to explicit algebraic realizations by twisted group doubles, providing a useful tool for classification and reconstruction in prime power dimension.

In particular, when a braided fusion category is integral, so that the Frobenius–Perron dimensions of all simple objects are integers, its global dimension often admits a prime-power factorization that is reflected in the internal tensor structure of the category. Under suitable hypotheses, nilpotence implies that the category can be built through successive extensions by finite groups, and in the braided integral case this frequently forces the category to be group-theoretical, meaning that it is Morita equivalent to a pointed fusion category. This relationship highlights a deep parallel between nilpotent fusion categories and nilpotent finite groups: just as a finite nilpotent group decomposes as a direct product of its Sylow subgroups, an integral braided nilpotent fusion category admits an analogue of Sylow decomposition into tensor factors whose Frobenius–Perron dimensions are powers of distinct primes. Such a decomposition not only clarifies the prime-local structure of the category but also provides a powerful mechanism for reducing questions about classification, modularity, and representation-theoretic invariants to the prime-power case. Consequently, the study of integral nilpotent braided fusion categories reveals a robust bridge between categorical tensor structures and classical finite group theory, with group-theoretical categories serving as the categorical analogue of groups whose representation theory is controlled by pointed data.

counterfactuals.prompt: State the main theorem and consequences of a paper on prime power dimensional modular categories, twisted doubles of finite p-groups, and the group-theoretical nature of semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras.
counterfactuals.output:
**Main theorem (prime-power modular categories).**  
Let \(\mathcal C\) be an **integral modular category** whose Frobenius–Perron dimension is a power of a prime,
\[
\operatorname{FPdim}(\mathcal C)=p^n .
\]
Then \(\mathcal C\) is **group-theoretical**.

Equivalently, such a modular category is Morita equivalent to a pointed fusion category \(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega\), where \(G\) is a finite \(p\)-group and \(\omega\in Z^3(G,\mathbb C^\times)\).

---

## Consequences

### 1. Prime-power integral modular categories come from finite \(p\)-groups

Since group-theoretical modular categories are realized as centers of pointed fusion categories, an integral modular category of dimension \(p^n\) is built from data of a finite \(p\)-group and a 3-cocycle. In particular, many such categories are braided equivalent to representation categories of **twisted Drinfeld doubles**
\[
\operatorname{Rep}\bigl(D^\omega(G)\bigr),
\]
or to closely related group-theoretical modular categories, with \(G\) a finite \(p\)-group.

Here \(D^\omega(G)\) denotes the twisted quantum double of \(G\), associated to a class
\[
\omega\in H^3(G,\mathbb C^\times).
\]

---

### 2. Twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups exhaust the centers

If \(\mathcal C=\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega\) is a pointed fusion category with \(G\) a finite \(p\)-group, then its Drinfeld center is modular and satisfies
\[
Z(\mathrm{Vec}_G^\omega)\simeq \operatorname{Rep}\bigl(D^\omega(G)\bigr).
\]
Thus the modular categories appearing as centers in prime-power dimension are precisely representation categories of twisted doubles of finite \(p\)-groups.

---

### 3. Semisimple quasi-Hopf algebras of dimension \(p^n\) are group-theoretical

Let \(H\) be a semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra over \(\mathbb C\) with
\[
\dim H=p^n .
\]
Then \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\) is a fusion category of prime-power dimension. Its Drinfeld center
\[
Z(\operatorname{Rep}(H))
\]
is an integral modular category of dimension \(p^{2n}\), hence group-theoretical by the main theorem. This implies that \(\operatorname{Rep}(H)\) itself is group-theoretical.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{Every semisimple quasi-Hopf algebra of prime-power dimension is group-theoretical.}}
\]

---

### 4. Structural implication

The theorem rules out exotic integral modular categories of prime-power dimension: they must arise from finite group data. In particular, prime-power dimensional integral modular categories are controlled by \(p\)-groups and group cohomology, rather than by genuinely new non-group-theoretical fusion data.
